topic: Space-Filling Curves: Bridging the Finite and the Infinite
target_audience: University students (STEM majors) or advanced high school students

sections.title: The Paradox of Dimensionality (0:00-0:45)
sections.content: Introduce the prerequisite: Dimensionality. Explain how we perceive 1D lines and 2D planes. Pose the counter-intuitive question: Can a 1D line ever perfectly fill a 2D square area?
sections.example: Visual: A long, flexible thread (1D) being coiled inside a square box (2D) until the box is completely 'filled' by the thread.

sections.title: Constructing the Peano Curve (0:45-2:00)
sections.content: Introduce the concept of iterative processes (recursion). Explain that while the curve is finite at any step n, it approaches an infinite limit. Use the Peano curve as the primary demonstration of mapping [0,1] to [0,1]x[0,1].
sections.example: Animation: Starting with a cross shape, progressively subdividing each segment into smaller crosses. Show how the 'wiggle' complexity increases with each iteration.

sections.title: The Infinite Limit: Breaking Topology (2:00-3:30)
sections.content: Explain the relationship between finite steps and the infinite limit. Discuss the concept of a 'limit curve.' Emphasize that while each iteration is a continuous function, the limit becomes a space-filling curve that is surjective (covers every point in the 2D plane).
sections.example: Visual transition: A character like 'Fractal Fox' tracing the path; as iterations increase to infinity, the fox's path turns from a simple line into a solid, colored square.

sections.title: Real-World Applications (3:30-4:30)
sections.content: Connect the theoretical math to modern technology. Explain how Hilbert curves are used in computer science for memory optimization, image processing, and antenna design.
sections.example: Application: A robot vacuum cleaner using a Hilbert curve pattern to ensure 100% floor coverage with no overlapping paths, demonstrating efficiency.

sections.title: Synthesis & Philosophical Reflection (4:30-5:00)
sections.content: Summarize how infinite mathematical processes reveal that the boundary between 1D and 2D is not as rigid as it seems. Encourage viewers to see infinity not as an impossible distance, but as a tool to describe physical reality.
sections.example: Final Graphic: A fading animation showing the transition from a single line to a dense, solid square, labeled 'The Infinite is merely the limit of the finite.'
